# Generative AI's Act Two: From Technology Hammer to Real Value

## Source
https://www.sequoiacap.com/article/generative-ai-act-two/

Published September 20, 2023 by Sonya Huang, Pat Grady and GPT-4 (Sequoia Capital)

## The Foundation: Decades of…51 tokens truncated…lops of data.
- **Four decades of the internet** (accelerated by COVID) produced trillions of tokens of training data.
- **Two decades of mobile and cloud computing** put a supercomputer in every human's palm.

ChatGPT's launch was the spark that ignited a Cambrian explosion of innovation not seen since the early internet. AI researchers became rockstars, hacker houses overflowed with autonomous agents and companionship chatbots, and the arXiv printing press became so prolific that researchers jokingly called for a pause on publications.

But excitement quickly turned to hysteria. Every company became an "AI copilot." Inboxes filled with undifferentiated pitches for "AI Salesforce" and "AI Adobe." The $100M pre-product seed round returned. Cracks appeared: artists challenged machine-generated IP, Washington debated regulation, and a whisper spread that generative AI was not actually useful — products fell short of expectations with terrible user retention.

## Early Commercial Traction Despite Skepticism

Despite the discontent, generative AI has had a more successful commercial start than SaaS, with **>$1 billion in revenue from startups alone** — a milestone that took SaaS years, not months, to reach. Standout successes include:

- **ChatGPT**: Fastest-growing application in history, with strong product-market fit among students and developers.
- **Midjourney**: Reported hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue with a team of just 11 people.
- **Character.ai**: Popularized AI entertainment and companionship; users spend an average of **2 hours per session** in-app.

However, these successes don't change the reality that many AI companies lack product-market fit or sustainable competitive advantage.

## The Retention Problem: AI-First Apps vs. Incumbents

Mobile app retention data reveals a stark gap between established consumer apps and AI-first companies:

### User Retention Comparison (Mobile Apps)

| App | Category | Retention Rate |
|---|---|---|
| WhatsApp | Incumbent | 85% |
| Instagram | Incumbent | 64% |
| YouTube | Incumbent | 64% |
| TikTok | Incumbent | 60% |
| Snapchat | Incumbent | 51% |
| Roblox | Incumbent | 41% |
| Tinder | Incumbent | 34% |
| Candy Crush | Incumbent | 32% |
| Duolingo | Incumbent | 30% |
| **Incumbent Median** | — | **51%** |
| Character.ai | AI-First | 41% |
| Runway | AI-First | 27% |
| Remini | AI-First | 14% |
| ChatGPT | AI-First | 14% |
| Lensa | AI-First | 12% |
| **AI-First Median** | — | **14%** |

![Retention comparison: Incumbents vs AI-First Companies](./assets/figure_2.jpg)

A separate monthly active usage benchmark for incumbents shows even higher engagement bars:

| App | Monthly Active Usage |
|---|---|
| YouTube | 85% |
| Instagram | 73% |
| TikTok | 69% |
| Snapchat | 67% |
| WhatsApp | 63% |
| Roblox | 61% |

| Duolingo | 50% |
| Candy Crush | 48% |
| **Median** | **63%** |

![Monthly active usage benchmarks for incumbents](./assets/figure_3.jpg)

## From Act 1 to Act 2

Sequoia frames the generative AI market as transitioning between two phases:

**Act 1 (Technology-Out):** The discovery of foundation models as a new "hammer" led to a wave of novelty apps — lightweight demonstrations of cool technology. These apps used foundation models as the entire solution and often lacked stickiness.

**Act 2 (Customer-Back):** The emerging phase focuses on solving human problems end-to-end. Key characteristics of Act 2 companies:

- Use foundation models as **a piece** of a more comprehensive solution, not the entire product
- Introduce **new editing interfaces** that make workflows stickier and outputs better
- Are often **multi-modal** in nature
- Solve problems **end-to-end** rather than offering thin wrappers

Examples of Act 2 companies: **Harvey** (custom LLMs for elite law firms), **Glean** (crawling and indexing workspaces for relevant enterprise AI), **Character** and **Ava** (digital companions).

The updated Sequoia generative AI market map is now organized **by use case rather than model modality**, reflecting the evolution from technology hammer to actual value delivery and the increasingly multi-modal nature of applications.

## Key Findings

- **Generative AI startups exceeded $1B in revenue faster than SaaS**, proving real commercial demand despite hype-cycle skepticism.
- **AI-first apps face a severe retention gap**: 14% median retention vs. 51% for incumbent consumer apps — a 3.6x disadvantage.
- **The market is shifting from Act 1 (technology-out) to Act 2 (customer-back)**, where foundation models become components of comprehensive, workflow-integrated solutions rather than standalone products.
- **Multi-modal, end-to-end problem solving** and new editing interfaces are the hallmarks of companies likely to win in Act 2.
- **Character.ai is the retention outlier** among AI-first apps at 41%, approaching incumbent levels, suggesting that companionship/entertainment may be generative AI's strongest consumer use case.

Targeting **executives / decision-makers**. Pyramid structure — every sentence carries information. Composed, authoritative, and insightful tone.

### Stage Direction Markers

- **Pyramid structure**: Conclusion → Arguments → Details
- **Data contextualization**: Every number has a comparison reference
- **Executive language**: "The strategic implication is...", "The core insight is..."

# 01_title_slide

[Transition] This deck frames Sequoia Capital's September 2023 analysis of generative AI's shift from novelty to value.

The core message is simple: Act 1 proved the technology and stimulated demand, but Act 2 will be decided by whether products solve real human problems with durable retention. [Pause]

Key points: (1) Generative AI has moved beyond demos (2) Investors and founders should evaluate retention and workflow ownership (3) The analysis is Sequoia Capital-attributed and data-forward
Duration: 1 minute
Flex: [If time is tight, move quickly to the convergence timeline]

# 02_decades_of_convergence

[Transition] Generative AI did not appear suddenly; it was enabled by decades of compounding technology progress.

Three waves converged. Six decades of Moore's Law produced zettascale compute and teraflops of data. Four decades of the internet produced trillions of tokens of training data. Two decades of mobile and cloud put a supercomputer in every human's palm. [Pause]

The strategic implication is that ChatGPT was the spark, not the foundation itself.

Key points: (1) Compute, data, and distribution converged (2) ChatGPT ignited the innovation wave (3) The opportunity rests on long-run infrastructure compounding
Duration: 2 minutes
Flex: [Skip the decade-by-decade details if the audience already knows the history]

# 03_genai_outpaces_saas

[Transition] The first commercial signal was unusually strong.

Generative AI startups exceeded $1 billion in revenue from startups alone in months, while SaaS took years to reach the same milestone. [Data] The brief highlights ChatGPT as the fastest-growing application in history, Midjourney with hundreds of millions in reported revenue and only 11 employees, and Character.ai with 2-hour average session time.

But revenue velocity does not by itself prove sustainable product-market fit. The next question is retention. [Pause]

Key points: (1) >$1B startup revenue proves real demand (2) ChatGPT, Midjourney, and Character.ai are standout examples (3) Revenue traction must be tested against retention
Duration: 2 minutes
Flex: [If time is tight, emphasize the >$1B milestone and transition]

# 04_retention_gap_incumbents_vs_ai

[Transition] The central problem appears when we compare retention.

Incumbent consumer apps show a 51% median retention rate. AI-first companies show a 14% median retention rate. [Benchmark] That is a 3.6x disadvantage for AI-first apps. [Pause]

Character.ai is the AI-first outlier at 41%, approaching incumbent levels, but the category median remains low. This is why novelty is not enough; repeated usage is the scarce asset.

Key points: (1) Incumbent median retention is 51% (2) AI-first median retention is 14% (3) Character.ai is an outlier, not yet the category norm
Duration: 3 minutes
Flex: [If time is tight, focus on the medians and Character.ai outlier]

# 05_incumbent_monthly_usage

[Transition] The incumbent benchmark is high not only in retention, but also in monthly active usage.

YouTube leads the benchmark at 85% monthly active usage, followed by Instagram at 73%, TikTok at 69%, Snapchat at 67%, and WhatsApp at 63%. The incumbent median is 63%. [Pause]

For AI applications, the bar is therefore not simply initial trial. The bar is repeated monthly habit formation.

Key points: (1) YouTube reaches 85% monthly active usage (2) The incumbent median is 63% (3) AI-first apps must create durable habits, not just viral launches
Duration: 2 minutes
Flex: [Skip individual app details and cite the median if time is constrained]

# 06_act1_vs_act2

[Transition] Sequoia's diagnosis is that Act 1 started technology-out, while Act 2 must be customer-back.

Act 1 treated foundation models as the entire solution. That produced novelty demos, lightweight wrappers, and poor retention. Act 2 treats foundation models as one piece of a comprehensive solution. It introduces new editing interfaces, supports multi-modal workflows, and solves problems end-to-end. [Pause]

The brief names Harvey, Glean, Character, and Ava as Act 2 exemplars.

Key points: (1) Act 1 equals technology hammer searching for nails (2) Act 2 equals customer-back problem solving (3) Harvey, Glean, Character, and Ava illustrate the shift
Duration: 3 minutes
Flex: [If time is tight, emphasize the left-right contrast]

# 07_market_map_evolution

[Transition] The market map also changes when the product logic changes.

Sequoia's updated generative AI market map is organized by use case rather than model modality. That means the old text, image, and code taxonomy gives way to human-problem categories such as legal, enterprise search, and companionship.

This reorganization mirrors the broader Act 1 to Act 2 transition: the market is moving from technology capability to value delivery. [Pause]

Key points: (1) Market map shifts from modality to use case (2) Act 2 applications are increasingly multi-modal (3) Use-case ownership is the strategic lens
Duration: 2 minutes
Flex: [If time is tight, use Harvey, Glean, Character, and Ava as examples only]

# 08_takeaways_for_builders_investors

[Transition] The actionable takeaway is that generative AI demand is real, but durable winners require a different underwriting lens.

First, retention is the critical challenge: 14% median for AI-first apps versus 51% for incumbents. Second, foundation models should be components, not the whole product. Third, multi-modal, workflow-integrated solutions will win. Fourth, the >$1B revenue milestone proves real demand exists despite hype cycles. Fifth, companies solving end-to-end human problems will define Act 2. [Pause]

Key points: (1) Underwrite retention (2) Prefer workflow-integrated solutions (3) Back customer-back teams solving complete problems
Duration: 2 minutes
Flex: [Use this slide as the close if discussion time is limited]
